new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement covering all 19 Lower Cross languages of the study, Ukwa included (recorded by Connell in 1988): two lexical tones H/L plus phonemic downstep (terraced-level tone languages); no word stress -- Ward's verb-root stress for Efik is rejected and LC is called 'a non-stress language'; only phrasal stress and stress-like marking of compound junctures are conceded, uninvestigated. Nothing is said about Ukwa prosody specifically.
new_statements.exceptions: Possible phrasal stress and stress at the juncture of compound elements (fn.32); Faraclas (1984b) analyses Obolo with phrasal stress and an extra-high tone; p.104 speculates that positional consonant weakening 'may be related to stress in Ibibio', unstudied.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the Lower Cross group as a whole, argued mainly from Efik/Ibibio data on citation forms; word-level stress denied, phrase-level stress left open. Ukwa itself is covered only by Connell's own 1988 wordlist recordings (consonant inventory Table 2.1a, cognate sets), with no Ukwa-specific prosodic remark.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is group-level (all Lower Cross languages, argued chiefly from Efik efik1245 and Ibibio ibib1240), not Ukwa-specific. Connell recorded Ukwa (Cross River State) himself in 1988 and treats it as arguably part of an Anaang-Efik-Ibibio-Ukwa dialect cluster with fairly high mutual intelligibility (thesis pp.5, 8-9, 14). No grammar, sketch or phonology of Ukwa itself exists in Glottolog or in any index searched.

sources.note: Ukwa is one of the 19 LC languages Connell recorded (p.5, p.14). Group-level only: LC languages are 'two-toned, terraced level languages' (sec. 2.2.2, p.47); Ward's (1933) verb-root stress for Efik rejected, 'difficult to find any true evidence for stress' (p.55); fn.32: not asserting 'no stress at all in Efik or the other LC languages' -- likely some phrasal stress and compound-juncture stress; fn.34 p.56 calls LC 'a non-stress language'. Nothing Ukwa-specific on prosody.

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce. 1994. The Lower Cross languages: a prolegomena to the classification of the Cross River languages. Journal of West African Languages 24(1): 3-46.
sources.note: Sec. 3.3 p.10: all LC languages have two tones H/L plus contrastive downstep, classic terracing; sec. 5 p.12: tonal systems 'further complicated through interaction with phrasal stress, but except for Faraclas (1984b) for Obolo, no investigation in this area has been done.' No word-stress statement; Ukwa appears only in consonant-inventory and cognate tables.
